boards.title: Only Happens Here: 10 Traditions That Make No Sense Anywhere Else
boards.description: Ten documented University of Kansas traditions, from Mount Oread ceremony to Jayhawk game-day rituals.

cards.title: Join the Rock Chalk Chant
cards.subtitle: University-wide yell rooted in Mount Oread limestone
cards.notes: Listen for the slow chant at a KU event, then join the repeated “Rock Chalk, Jayhawk, KU” cadence with the crowd.
cards.short_summary: KU’s signature cheer began as a student yell in the 1880s.
cards.evidence_claim: KU Athletics states that Rock Chalk was adopted as the college yell in 1886 and was known as the school’s official yell by fall 1887.
cards.access_notes: Participation depends on the event; follow venue and event guidance.

cards.title: Wave the Wheat
cards.subtitle: Synchronized arm-waving at KU sporting events
cards.notes: At the appropriate game moment, raise both arms and move them side to side with the crowd to evoke a wheat field.
cards.short_summary: A sea of waving arms turns KU crowds into a field-of-wheat visual.
cards.evidence_claim: KU describes Waving the Wheat as a tradition in which a large group waves hands side to side, resembling wheat in the wind.
cards.source_title: Wave the Wheat Wall | KU Memorial Unions
cards.access_notes: Use the gesture at designated moments during sporting events.

cards.title: Walk Down the Hill at Commencement
cards.subtitle: Graduates’ ceremonial descent from Mount Oread
cards.notes: If graduating, follow the commencement procession from Memorial Drive through the Campanile and onward to Memorial Stadium.
cards.short_summary: KU frames the graduate walk down Mount Oread as commencement’s centerpiece.
cards.evidence_claim: KU Commencement calls the ceremonial walk down Mount Oread its most treasured tradition and says it begins on Memorial Drive.
cards.access_notes: For graduating students participating in KU Commencement; consult the current ceremony instructions.

cards.title: Save the Campanile Passage for Graduation
cards.subtitle: Memorial Campanile, Mount Oread
cards.notes: Treat the Campanile passage as part of the graduation milestone: KU notes that superstitious students avoid it until Commencement.
cards.short_summary: The commencement route gives a campus superstition a ceremonial payoff.
cards.evidence_claim: KU Commencement says superstitious students avoid marching through Memorial Campanile until Commencement.
cards.access_notes: Respect the site and use public routes; the ceremonial passage is part of Commencement.

cards.title: Wear Crimson and Blue
cards.subtitle: KU’s official athletic colors
cards.notes: Use crimson and blue when showing KU spirit at campus gatherings or athletics events; KU traces their official athletic adoption to 1896.
cards.short_summary: The color pairing is a long-running visual marker of KU identity.
cards.evidence_claim: KU Athletics states that the KU Athletic Board adopted crimson and blue as the university’s official team colors in May 1896.
cards.access_notes: Personal attire is optional; comply with any event-specific policies.

cards.title: Learn “I’m a Jayhawk”
cards.subtitle: KU fight song associated with athletics traditions
cards.notes: Follow the band or crowd at an event and learn the fight song by listening first; its history is documented by Kansas Athletics.
cards.short_summary: A 1912 song that became popular with KU students in 1920.
cards.evidence_claim: KU Athletics says “I’m a Jayhawk,” written in 1912 by KU graduate George Bowles, became popular with KU students in 1920.
cards.access_notes: Participation depends on the event; follow band and venue guidance.

cards.entity_name: The Crimson and the Blue Alma Mater
cards.title: Sing “The Crimson and the Blue”
cards.subtitle: KU’s alma mater
cards.notes: At a tradition-focused gathering, listen for the alma mater and join only if you know the words; KU commonly pairs it with Rock Chalk.
cards.short_summary: KU’s alma mater predates many current campus rituals.
cards.evidence_claim: KU Memorial Unions states that KU’s alma mater, “The Crimson and the Blue,” was written in 1891 and is usually followed by the Rock Chalk Chant.
cards.access_notes: Participation depends on the event; follow the event program and performers.

cards.title: Spot Big Jay
cards.subtitle: KU’s 3-D Jayhawk mascot
cards.notes: Look for Big Jay at a KU athletics or spirit event and enjoy the mascot’s role in the school’s Jayhawk visual tradition.
cards.short_summary: Big Jay brought the Jayhawk from illustration into mascot form.
cards.evidence_claim: KU Athletics states that the KU Alumni Association provided a Jayhawk mascot costume in the 1960s, introducing Big Jay.
cards.access_notes: Mascot appearances vary by event; do not enter restricted performance areas.

cards.title: Remember Baby Jay’s Homecoming Debut
cards.subtitle: 1971 halftime Jayhawk-mascot milestone
cards.notes: Use a KU traditions display or athletics history page to see the origin story: Baby Jay was introduced from a huge egg at Homecoming.
cards.short_summary: A halftime reveal added Baby Jay to KU’s mascot family.
cards.evidence_claim: KU Athletics reports that fans saw Big Jay’s companion, Baby Jay, hatch from a huge egg at 1971 Homecoming halftime.
cards.access_notes: Historical tradition; current Homecoming programming may differ.

cards.title: Start Hawk Week at Traditions Night
cards.subtitle: Memorial Stadium welcome-week tradition session
cards.notes: Attend the listed Hawk Week session to learn KU traditions in Memorial Stadium; check the current schedule and any participation instructions.
cards.short_summary: A fall welcome-week event explicitly devoted to KU traditions.
cards.evidence_claim: KU’s Hawk Week page lists Traditions Night and describes it as an opportunity to catch Jayhawk spirit and learn KU traditions.
cards.source_title: Hawk Week | KU Center for Orientation & Transition Programs
cards.access_notes: Scheduled for Hawk Week; confirm date, location, accessibility details, and requirements on the current page.
